paragraphs.heading: Charge pulled apart
paragraphs.text: In chemistry, polarity means electric charge is separated within a molecule or a group inside it, giving it a negative end and a positive end. This is described as having an electric dipole moment. A polar molecule must contain at least one polar bond, which comes from a difference in electronegativity between the joined atoms. Polar molecules attract one another through dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. Polarity shapes surface tension, solubility, and melting and boiling points.

paragraphs.heading: The pull on electrons
paragraphs.text: Atoms do not all attract electrons equally hard. The strength of an atom's pull on its electrons is called its electronegativity. Fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen pull strongly, while the alkali and alkaline earth metals pull weakly. In a bond, the electrons are drawn closer to the atom with the higher electronegativity, so the sharing is lopsided. Since electrons carry negative charge, this creates a dipole, a split between positive and negative charge.

paragraphs.heading: Partial charges
paragraphs.text: The charge separated in such a dipole is usually smaller than one fundamental charge, so it is called a partial charge, written δ⁺ and δ⁻. Christopher Ingold and Edith Hilda Ingold introduced these symbols in 1926. The bond dipole moment is the separated charge multiplied by the distance between the charges. The SI unit, the coulomb–meter, is too large to be handy for molecules, so chemists use the debye, written D. One debye equals 3.33564×10⁻³⁰ C·m.

paragraphs.heading: From nonpolar to ionic
paragraphs.text: Bonds sit on a scale between completely nonpolar and completely polar. A completely nonpolar bond forms when the two electronegativities are identical. A completely polar bond is better called an ionic bond: the difference is so large that one atom pulls an electron right away from its partner. The words polar and nonpolar are normally kept for covalent bonds, where the polarity is not complete. Pauling estimated that a bond whose atoms differ in electronegativity by 1.7 has 50% ionic character, so a wider gap gives a mostly ionic bond.

paragraphs.heading: Two-atom molecules
paragraphs.text: A molecule made of two atoms has only one bond, single or multiple, so the dipole of that bond is the dipole of the whole molecule. Typical values run from 0 to 11 D. Bromine, Br₂, is symmetric and has no dipole moment at all. Potassium bromide gas, KBr, is highly ionic and sits near the other end, at 10.41 D.

paragraphs.heading: Shape matters
paragraphs.text: In a molecule with several bonds, the total dipole can be estimated by adding the bond dipoles together as vectors. So polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule: if the bond dipoles cancel out by symmetry, the molecule has no overall polarity. A molecule can also be polar because nonpolar bonds and non-bonding electron pairs are arranged unevenly. Labels such as polar covalent and nonpolar covalent are often relative, meaning one molecule is simply more or less polar than another.
